content.text: Starting this week and ongoing for the next 15 weeks or so, we will be doing weekly sprints! A sprint is a development iteration cycle in the agile project framework. We’ll be doing a somewhat simplified version of this in that we’ll combine a few different steps together.
As a simplification, you can do  1+3 in one big team meeting, since you are really recapping the week and then planning the next.
Issues and Scope and Assignment Q/A
❓ When should you use GitHub issues?
✅ ALWAYS! This is a big part of how we’ll be grading - and is a huge timesaver for your team in the long run.
❓ What is the right scope for an issue?

✅ Each issue should be scoped to be around 1 sitdown work session, just a couple hours. Break up large tasks into individual smaller ones, each one should be under a few hours of work. You can think of issues as individual tasks: “create login button”, “api endpoint for user profile”, etc. Issues can also be bugs that you find along the way. Convert large tasks into

. The smaller the tasks the actually faster you will work (not just the appearance of speed). It is easier to take on a manageable scope issue and work through it than if the issue has multiple steps that quickly become overwhelming to think through.
❓ Should I assign my teammates to issues?

✅ Yes! You should assign people to each issue as you work on them so your team knows who is doing what. Feel free to assign each other tasks, a little aggressiveness is ok! Keep it to 1 teammate per issue.
❓ Can I use comments on issues to coordinate with my team?

✅ Yes! You can interact via comments on the issues, on a good project the board will feel like a community, people upvoting and clapping for each other, discussing the issues, or how best to implement something. EC: mention
in an issue or a PR when you need help or feedback or want to say hi. We’re happy to help — and since this was a wall of text we’ll know that you happened to read it all.
❓ Can I just use groupme to tell people what to do?
⛔️ No! You can discuss things to do for sure, but you should always use zenhub to keep track of who is working on what. Also you should be using Slack not groupme, we’re all in this together.
❓ Can I just use todos posted in slack to tell people what to do?
⛔️ No! You can discuss things to do for sure, but you should always use zenhub to keep track of who is working on what.
❓ I’ve used Jira/other brand before, why can’t we use that?

⛔️ Sorry, but we’re going to stick to one task manager. For all practical purposes Jira/Asana/Trello/ZenHub all have many overlapping features - GitHub projects is conveniently right in GitHub, which means you can spend more of your time there, rather than switching between a lot of tools. The important part is the agile workflow of moving tickets between stages and they all do it the same way.

🚀 Remember a part of your grade is usage of issues - once your project gets rolling you should shoot aim for closing 4+ issues per week per person. This should give you a sense of the scope of an issue. If each issue is under 2 hrs then 5 issues is around 10 hours. This isn’t a hard and fast rule - but try to do this on average. Issues should not take up a team member’s time or mental bandwidth; putting ideas into the Later Pipeline gets them out of the way and helps teams focus on immediate priorities.

, but we’ll simplify and just call that whole stack Nexts. If an issue doesn’t have a Milestone/Sprint assigned, you can consider them part of your “product backlog”. Once you add a Milestone, they become part of your “sprint backlog” (that is, the tasks that you’ll complete in an upcoming sprint.) The process of keeping this pipeline organized is known as “backlog refinement”, we’ll do something a bit simpler and do all of this during a team retrospective meeting.

This is the answer to, “What are you doing now?” Ideally, each team member should be working on just one thing at a time. Tasks here should be ordered by priority with Assignees added.

and make it an iteration type that starts on this next Monday!  We’ll do Monday - Sunday sprints and make the Sprints 1 week long.

Well yes, you gotta make progress right? Gotta make it to DEMOS! If every issue takes 2 hours (a nice casual sitdown work session), then there are you are at 8 hours. That leaves a few hours for things taking a bit longer to do / team meetings and discussions.

If you prefer you are more than welcome to use Estimates to track how much time you as a team estimate the tasks instead of the 4 issues method.  This allows you to be more flexible with # of issues, as long as the story points assigned to someone add up to around 8-10.
Whenever we do feedback on designs we’ll be leaving comments in Figma. You should enter in all the actionable design feedback items into your project board and add them to this sprint to resolve.

✋ What do you mean “resolve”? Well, you should at least respond to each Figma comment with some words, but in most cases this means updating your designs to correspond with your current plans as well as any changes that came up in discussion, or in the grading feedback for mockups.
And a couple of small things

Make sure your README.md files are updated with the current installation and deployment instructions as well as any architecture changes. This will be a small part of every sprint, you should always keep it up to date as the README is where your graders start to get it running locally for testing.
